config.title: Build centralized error handler middleware

intro.title: Build centralized error handler middleware
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a centralized error handler middleware for a Node.js application. You'll learn how to create a function that catches errors from your routes and processes them in one place, making your code cleaner and more maintainable. The core concept involves using Express middleware and JavaScript's error handling constructs like try-catch and custom error objects. You'll work with Node.js, Express, and middleware functions to implement this essential backend pattern.
intro.usecase: Centralized error handling is essential in production Node.js applications like e-commerce platforms, banking systems, and SaaS dashboards. For example, when a payment form submission fails in an online store, a centralized handler can catch the error, log it for debugging, and return a user-friendly message instead of crashing the server. In analytics dashboards, this middleware ensures that API errors from data-fetching endpoints are consistently formatted and logged, maintaining system stability while providing clear feedback to users. Developers implement this pattern to prevent server crashes, standardize error responses across all routes, and simplify debugging in complex applications.

objectives: Construct a custom error class that extends the built-in Error object
Implement a centralized error handling middleware function in Express.js
Configure the middleware to catch both operational and programming errors
Manipulate error responses to provide consistent structure across the API
Integrate the error handler as the last middleware in the Express application
Initialize error instances with appropriate HTTP status codes and messages
Apply the error handler to differentiate between development and production environments

steps.title: Import required modules for error handling
steps.instruction: Import the http-status-codes module for standardized HTTP status codes.
steps.hint: Use the require statement to import the module. The module name is 'http-status-codes'.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: importing a module
const express = require('express');
steps.expectedOutcome: The http-status-codes module is imported and ready to use for HTTP status codes.
successCriteria: The http-status-codes module is imported using require.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're importing the correct module name.
steps.feedbackWrong: The import statement is missing or incorrect. Try using: const statusCodes = require('http-status-codes');

steps.title: Create the error handler middleware function
steps.instruction: Create a function named errorHandler that takes four parameters: err, req, res, and next.
steps.hint: Define a function with the exact name 'errorHandler' and list the four parameters in parentheses.
steps.seedCode:
// Import the http-status-codes module here

// Create the errorHandler function here
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have an errorHandler function defined with the correct parameters, ready to be implemented in later steps.
successCriteria: The errorHandler function is defined with err, req, res, and next as parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function is named exactly 'errorHandler' and includes all four parameters: err, req, res, and next.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to create a function named 'errorHandler' with parameters (err, req, res, next).

steps.title: Set default status code for errors
steps.instruction: Inside the errorHandler function, set a default status code of 500 (Internal Server Error) if err.statusCode is not provided. Use an if statement to check if err.statusCode exists.
steps.hint: Check if the error object has a statusCode property. If it doesn't, assign 500 to err.statusCode.
steps.expectedOutcome: The errorHandler function should now include logic to set a default status code of 500 when err.statusCode is missing.
successCriteria: The errorHandler function contains an if statement that checks if err.statusCode is falsy and sets it to 500.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check your condition. Make sure you're checking if err.statusCode doesn't exist and setting it to 500.
steps.feedbackWrong: The default status code logic is missing or incorrect. Remember to check if err.statusCode exists and set it to 500 if it doesn't.

steps.title: Define error response structure
steps.instruction: Inside the errorHandler function, create a response object with status, message, and stack properties based on the error parameter.
steps.hint: Define a variable like 'errorResponse' that contains an object with keys for status, message, and stack. Use err.status, err.message, and err.stack for the values.
steps.expectedOutcome: The errorHandler function will have a response object that structures error information consistently.
successCriteria: A response object is defined inside errorHandler with status, message, and stack properties derived from the err parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your response object includes all three properties: status, message, and stack, each using values from the err parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The response object is missing or incomplete. Inside errorHandler, define an object with status, message, and stack properties based on the error.

steps.title: Send error response to client
steps.instruction: Inside the errorHandler function, use res.status().json() to send the error response with the appropriate status code.
steps.hint: Call res.status() with the status code variable, then chain .json() with the error response object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The errorHandler function will now send a structured JSON error response to the client when an error occurs.
successCriteria: The errorHandler function uses res.status().json() to send the error response with the appropriate status code.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using both res.status() and .json() methods together to send the complete error response.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error handler isn't sending responses correctly. Remember to use res.status().json() with the status code and error response object.

steps.title: Create a custom error class
steps.instruction: Create a custom error class named AppError that extends the built-in Error class. The class should accept statusCode and message parameters in its constructor.
steps.hint: Use the 'class' keyword to define AppError, extend Error, and set up a constructor that takes statusCode and message.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a custom AppError class that can be used to create errors with specific status codes and messages.
successCriteria: AppError class is defined, extends Error, and has a constructor that accepts statusCode and message parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the AppError class, but it's missing some required elements. Make sure it extends Error and has a constructor that accepts both statusCode and message parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The AppError class is not properly defined. Remember to use the 'class' keyword, extend Error, and create a constructor that takes statusCode and message parameters.

steps.title: Add constructor to custom error class
steps.instruction: Inside the AppError class, implement a constructor method that accepts statusCode and message parameters, calls super() with the message, and sets this.statusCode to the provided statusCode.
steps.hint: The constructor should take two parameters: statusCode and message. Call super(message) to pass the message to the parent Error class, then assign this.statusCode = statusCode.
steps.expectedOutcome: The AppError class will have a constructor that properly initializes statusCode and message properties.
successCriteria: AppError has a constructor with statusCode and message parameters, calls super(message), and sets this.statusCode.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your constructor calls super(message) and sets this.statusCode.
steps.feedbackWrong: The constructor is missing or incomplete. It should accept statusCode and message, call super(message), and set this.statusCode.

steps.title: Create a route that throws an error
steps.instruction: Create a GET route '/test-error' that throws a new AppError with status 400 and a test message.
steps.hint: Use the AppError class you created earlier to throw an error with status 400 and a message like 'Test error message'.
steps.expectedOutcome: A route that throws an AppError with status 400 when accessed.
successCriteria: The route '/test-error' is defined as a GET route and throws a new AppError with status 400 and a test message.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a route, but make sure it throws a new AppError with status 400 and a test message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route is not correctly defined or doesn't throw an AppError with the specified status and message.

steps.title: Register the error handler middleware
steps.instruction: Add the errorHandler middleware after all route definitions using app.use() in your Express application.
steps.hint: In Express, error-handling middleware should be added last, after all other app.use() and route calls. Use app.use(errorHandler).
steps.expectedOutcome: The errorHandler middleware is properly registered to catch errors from all routes.
successCriteria: The errorHandler middleware is added using app.use(errorHandler) after all route definitions.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're adding the errorHandler middleware after all route definitions.
steps.feedbackWrong: The error handler middleware isn't properly registered. Remember to use app.use(errorHandler) after all routes.

steps.title: Test the error handling system
steps.instruction: Start the Express server and test the '/test-error' route by making a GET request to see the structured error response.
steps.hint: Use app.listen() to start the server on a port (e.g., 3000) and then access http://localhost:3000/test-error in your browser or API client.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server starts successfully, and accessing '/test-error' returns a structured JSON error response with status 400 and the message 'Test error message'.
successCriteria: The server is started with app.listen() and the '/test-error' route returns the structured error response defined in the errorHandler.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the server, but make sure the '/test-error' route is accessible and returns the structured error response as defined in errorHandler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server may not be starting correctly or the '/test-error' route isn't returning the expected error response. Check your app.listen() call and ensure the errorHandler is properly registered.
